transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it's nice to meet you too. So, I guess... well, it's a bit of a long story, but what really made me finally make the appointment and come in today is that I've just been noticing this really unsettling shift in myself. 

You see, I've always been a very engaged, organized person. I'm an executive assistant, so keeping a pristine, perfectly managed calendar is basically my whole life, and usually, I get a real sense of satisfaction and pride from doing it well. But lately, even just looking at my schedule or trying to organize my week feels... I don't know, just completely flat. The whole thing just feels incredibly heavy. 

And it's not just work, which is the most concerning part to me, because it's spilling over into everything that usually makes me feel like myself. Like, I normally do these photography walks on the weekends—mostly urban architecture, I've been doing it for years, it's my main creative outlet and it usually clears my head—and I also mentor some kids at the local youth center on Tuesday evenings. Usually, I'm the one rallying everyone, setting the dates, getting things going. But recently, I just... I stopped initiating any of it. The camera is just sitting on my desk gathering dust, and I haven't reached out to the youth center in weeks. The idea of going out, or even just making the effort to start an activity, it just feels like wading through wet cement. It's this heavy, flat emptiness, and I just can't seem to muster the spark to start doing the things I actually care about anymore. It's just not like me at all to stop engaging with my own life like this, so I figured I really needed to come in and figure out what's going on.
Did this start after a major stressful life event or big change?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it didn't happen overnight, like a light switch flipping, but if I trace it back... it really started about a year and three months ago. Give or take a couple of weeks, but right around then. And it was definitely tied to a big change, a really stressful one. 

My brother, he... well, his health took a really sudden turn. And it wasn't just physical, his whole behavior started changing, becoming really unpredictable and difficult to manage. And because of the nature of my job, you know, being an executive assistant, I'm the organized one in the family. I'm the one who handles the logistics, the schedules, the crisis management. So, naturally, it all fell on me to coordinate everything for him. The doctors' appointments, the specialists, figuring out his insurance, managing his daily care needs, trying to keep the rest of the family updated without causing a panic... it was like taking on a second, incredibly demanding, full-time job. 

And at first, I was just running on adrenaline, just powering through it, making the spreadsheets, making the calls. But then, as the months dragged on—and like I said, it's been about a year and three months now of this constant, low-grade (and sometimes high-grade) crisis mode—that's when I started to feel this... this draining of my own energy. It was like I was pouring so much of my executive function into managing his life that there was just absolutely nothing left for mine. And that's when the photography stopped, and the youth center, and just... everything else. So yes, it definitely started after that whole situation with my brother began, and I just haven't been able to bounce back since.
Has this been going on continuously for more than six months?

Oh, yes, absolutely. Like I was just mentioning a moment ago, it’s been about a year and three months now. And when you ask if it's been continuous, I mean... yes, painfully continuous. It's not like I have a good week where I suddenly feel like myself again and then a bad week. 

Ever since my brother's health and his whole behavior took that dive and I had to step in to coordinate everything for him... it's just been this constant, unending stretch. Being someone who practically lives inside a calendar for a living, I track time very, very closely, so I know exactly how long it's been. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, you know? Like, maybe a Tuesday will roll around and I'll wake up and think, "Hey, I want to grab my camera today and go shoot those new buildings downtown," but... no. It's been every single day, week after week, month after month, for well over a year now. Fifteen months, give or take, of just... this. I haven't had a single reprieve since I took on all that extra weight with his care. It's just a straight, unbroken line on the calendar of feeling completely drained.
During this time, have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day?

You know, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that, because... well, I’ve actually spent a lot of time analyzing that precise distinction in my own head. Being an assistant, I'm very particular about words and what they mean. And when I hear the word 'depressed' or 'down,' I immediately picture, you know, someone crying all the time, or feeling this profound, crushing sadness, or maybe feeling worthless or guilty about things. And honestly? I don't really have that. 

I'm not sitting at my desk weeping over my boss's travel itinerary, you know? I don't feel sad in that deep, dark way. I mean, obviously, I feel a normal amount of sadness about my brother's health, because it's a tragic situation, but it's not this overwhelming black cloud of despair that follows me around all day. It’s actually... it's more like someone just unplugged my power cord from the wall. It’s an absence of feeling rather than a negative feeling, if that makes any sense at all? 

Like, I'll be sitting there, looking at an email from the youth center, and I don't feel down about it, I just feel... nothing. It's just a void. A heavy, blank void. I've had friends ask me if I'm depressed lately, and I always have to explain this whole exact thing to them, too, because they see me not taking my architecture photos and they just assume I'm sitting in a dark room crying. But I'm really not. I'm just... existing, I guess. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed most of the day. It's just that total, flat emptiness I was talking about.
Have you been crying more than usual lately?

No, not at all. And it's interesting you ask that right after the depression question, because it really reinforces what I was just trying to explain about this whole... void I've been stuck in. 

If anything, I'm crying less than I normally would. Or maybe not less, but just... not at all. You know, I'm a guy who usually gets a little misty-eyed at a good movie, or even a particularly touching long-distance commercial, you know? I'm not afraid to admit that. I've always been relatively in touch with my emotions. But lately? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. 

Even with everything going on with my brother—and there have been some objectively heartbreaking moments there, times where I've had to sit in these awful, sterile hospital waiting rooms for hours on end, just me and my laptop, coordinating his care while he's going through some really rough, unpredictable patches—I haven't shed a single tear. It’s like the mechanism for it is just broken or, I don't know, turned off entirely. 

I remember sitting there just last month, staring at this incredibly complex insurance denial form for one of his specialists. It was the kind of bureaucratic nightmare that, a year and a half ago, would normally have had me either furious or in tears from the sheer, overwhelming frustration of it all. And I just... stared at it. Dry eyes. Just completely flat. I didn't feel the urge to cry, I didn't feel a lump in my throat, nothing. So no, no extra crying. If anything, I'm almost a little disturbed by how dry my eyes have been through this whole ordeal, because you'd think I'd be weeping into my spreadsheets on a weekly basis with the amount of stress I'm under, but I'm just... not. The tears just aren't there.
Even if you don’t feel sad, have you been feeling hopeless?

Hopeless... no, no I wouldn't use that word either. It’s funny, because when you say 'hopeless,' I think of someone who has just completely thrown in the towel, you know? Someone who looks at the future and sees absolutely nothing, or thinks there's no point in even trying to move forward. And that’s really not me. 

I mean, just look at my day-to-day life. As an executive assistant, my entire career is literally built on the future—planning it, anticipating it, making sure everything is lined up for next week, next month, next quarter. I'm currently booking flights and hotels for a conference my boss is attending eight months from now. If I were truly hopeless, I don't think I could do that. I'd probably look at that calendar and think, "What's the point? None of this matters." But I don't. I still know the future is coming, and I still believe things will happen. 

And with my brother, too. I mean, I was just talking about those insurance denials a second ago. If I felt hopeless, I would have just crumpled up that denial letter and tossed it in the recycling bin under my desk, right? I would have just accepted that they weren't going to pay for his specialist and given up on the whole system. But I didn't. I filed an appeal. I drafted a very thorough three-page letter, I gathered all his medical records, I highlighted the relevant policy clauses... I did all of that because I still have hope that the appeal will go through. I still expect things to function, eventually, if I just put the right pieces in the right places. 

So, it's not a lack of hope. I know things can get better, or at least that time will keep moving forward and situations will resolve. It’s just... like I said before, I just don't have any emotional reaction to any of it while it's happening. I'm going through the motions of hoping, I'm doing all the administrative tasks a hopeful person does, I'm just doing them with a completely empty tank. So no, definitely not hopeless. Just... flat. Does that make sense? Because I really think there's a huge, fundamental difference between having no hope and just having no... no spark, I guess you could call it.
